Disclaimer and How to Read This Document
Educational use only. QuantTerminal is built for learning and research. It does not give investment advice
and it does not tell you what to buy or sell. This dashboard is for educational purposes only, and we are not
liable for any investment decisions made by users.
Why the labels say Bullish, Bearish and Neutral
Many tools show Buy, Sell or Hold. QuantTerminal does not. It uses three neutral words that only describe
what the numbers show:
Label
What it means
What it does NOT mean
Strongly Bullish / Bullish
Indicators lean upward right now
A promise the price will rise
Neutral
Indicators are mixed or flat
A promise nothing will change
Bearish / Strongly Bearish
Indicators lean downward right now
A promise the price will fall
How to read this document
• Plain language: each idea is explained in simple words first, then the technical name is shown.
• Screenshots were taken from the live app at quantterminal.streamlit.app.
• Currency: Indian stocks show the rupee sign, US stocks show the dollar sign.
• Market data means price and volume data collected from data providers such as Yahoo Finance.
Important limits to remember
• Past results do not guarantee future results.
• Every model is a simplification. It can be wrong.
• Data can be late, missing or revised by the provider.
• Always do your own research and talk to a qualified adviser before investing.

About This Project
What is QuantTerminal?
QuantTerminal is a free web app that lets you study the stock market using maths, statistics and machine
learning. You pick a stock, and the app draws charts, runs tests, builds forecasts, simulates the future and
can even write a 20-page research report for you.
The problem it solves
Professional analysis usually needs many separate tools: one for charts, one for statistics, one for
backtesting, one for reports. They are expensive and hard to learn. QuantTerminal puts all of them in one
place, with the same stock selected across every page.
Who is it for?
User
How they can use it
Students
Learn finance and data science with real market data
Beginner analysts
Practise research steps from charts to risk to reports
Researchers
Test ideas quickly and export results
Teachers
Show live examples in class
Core promises
• No look-ahead bias: tests only use information that was available at that time.
• No fake numbers: if data is missing, the app says so instead of inventing values.
• Open method: formulas and assumptions are written down in the docs folder.
• Educational focus: results describe history and do not give advice.
At a glance
Modules
20 workspaces (19 analysis pages plus Credits)
Domains
7 research domains
Code size
About 67,000 lines of Python
Tests
23 automated test files
Data
Daily prices for NSE, BSE, NYSE and NASDAQ stocks

Terminal Use Cases
Six common ways to use QuantTerminal.
Use case 1: Equity Research and Screening
Goal: Find and understand companies.
What you do
• Use Market Explorer presets to shortlist stocks.
• Open the Dashboard for price, valuation and returns.
• Check Technical Analysis for trend and momentum.
Example
A student wants large IT companies with rising
momentum. They filter by sector and RSI, then
compare two of them side by side.
Use case 2: Risk Measurement and Stress Testing
Goal: Understand how much could be lost.
What you do
• Read VaR and CVaR in Risk Analytics.
• Study drawdown depth and recovery time.
• Run Monte Carlo to see a range of outcomes.
Example
An analyst asks 'what is a bad month for this stock?'
and reads the 95% VaR and the worst historical
drawdown.
Use case 3: Strategy Design and Backtesting
Goal: Test a rule before believing in it.
What you do
• Build or pick a rule in Strategy Lab.
• Replay it in Backtesting with costs.
• Compare it with buy-and-hold.
Example
A learner tests an RSI rule and finds it loses after
brokerage costs, which teaches why costs matter.

11
Method and Bias Controls
A bias is a hidden mistake that makes results look better than they really are. The project lists its controls
in docs/BIAS_MITIGATION.md. Here are the most important ones in plain words.
Problem
Simple explanation
What QuantTerminal does
Look-ahead bias
Using tomorrow's information
today
Signals are lagged by one day and features only use
the past
Data leakage in ML
Test data sneaks into training
Time-ordered 80/20 split, scalers fitted on training
data only
Overfitting
Model memorises the past
Out-of-sample scores, walk-forward tests, warnings
on tuning
Unrealistic backtests
Ignoring costs
Brokerage and slippage are included
Spurious regression
Two trending series look related
by chance
Stationarity checks before regression
Survivorship
Only looking at companies that
survived
Limitations are stated clearly in the docs
Fake data
Filling gaps with invented values
No synthetic infilling
Core formulas used across the app
Measure
Plain meaning
Formula
Return
Percent change in price
(Pt - Pt-1) / Pt-1
Sharpe ratio
Return per unit of risk
(mean return - risk-free) / std dev x sqrt(252)
Sortino ratio
Return per unit of downside
risk
(mean return - risk-free) / downside std dev
Max drawdown
Worst fall from a peak
min( equity / running peak - 1 )
VaR (historical)
Loss not exceeded on most
days
Percentile of past returns
CAGR
Average yearly growth
(final / initial)1/years - 1
Even with these controls, every result is a historical study. Controls reduce mistakes but cannot predict the
future.

Module 03   Technical Analysis   Market & Data
A chart workstation for technical indicators. Indicators are simple formulas built from price and volume
that help describe trend, speed and volatility.
Technical Analysis page (live app)
What you can do
• Draw Bollinger Bands, moving averages and
SuperTrend on a candlestick chart
• Read momentum with RSI, Stochastic and MACD
• Measure volatility with ATR and Keltner channels
• Open 'playbooks' that explain how each indicator
family is usually read
How to read it
RSI above 70 is often called overbought and below 30
oversold. These are hints, not certainties.
Watch out
Indicators lag behind price and can give false signals in
sideways markets. Use several together.
Module 04   Statistical Analysis   Statistics & Returns
Shows how a stock's returns are spread out. It answers: are the returns 'normal', how fat are the tails, and
how do stocks move together?
Statistical Analysis page (live app)
What you can do
• See skewness (lean) and kurtosis (fat tails)
• Run normality tests (Jarque-Bera, Shapiro-Wilk)
• View histograms, KDE curves and Q-Q plots
• Build correlation matrices between stocks
How to read it
If the Q-Q plot points follow the straight line, returns
look normal. Big curves at the ends mean fat tails.
Watch out
Real stock returns are rarely perfectly normal. Test
results depend on how much history you pick.

Module 06   Volatility Lab   Statistics & Returns
Volatility means how much a price jumps around. This lab measures it in five ways and forecasts it with
GARCH models.
Volatility Lab page (live app)
What you can do
• Compare 5 estimators: Close-to-Close, Parkinson,
Garman-Klass, Rogers-Satchell, Yang-Zhang
• Fit GARCH(1,1) to see volatility clusters
• Use volatility cones to judge if today's volatility is
high or low
• View the volatility term structure
How to read it
A cone shows the normal range for volatility. If today's
value sits above the cone, volatility is unusually high.
Watch out
GARCH needs enough data to work well. Estimators that
use high and low prices are only as good as that data.

Module 07   Regime Detection   Forecasting & AI
Markets behave differently in calm and stormy times. A Hidden Markov Model (HMM) finds these hidden
'regimes' automatically.
Regime Detection page (live app)
What you can do
• Choose 2 or 3 regimes (for example calm, normal,
stressed)
• See the average return and risk of each regime
• View the chance of switching from one regime to
another
• Compare a regime strategy with simple
buy-and-hold
How to read it
Look at the coloured price chart: each colour is one
regime. The transition table tells you how long a regime
tends to last.
Watch out
Regimes are labelled after the fact using the full
sample, so they describe history. They are not a live
prediction tool.
Module 08   Factor Research   Portfolio & Research
Explains where a stock's returns come from: the overall market or something unique to the stock.
Factor Research page (live app)
What you can do
• Estimate Beta (how strongly a stock follows the
market)
• Estimate Jensen's Alpha (return beyond what beta
explains)
• Run style regressions inspired by Fama-French
• Watch rolling beta change over time
How to read it
Beta of 1 moves with the market, above 1 moves more,
below 1 moves less. R-squared tells you how much the
market explains.
Watch out
Alpha estimates can be noisy. Check the confidence
values before trusting them.

backtest
How to read it
A Z-score near 0 means the pair is normal. Large
positive or negative values mean the gap is stretched.
Watch out
Pairs can stop moving together. A pair that worked in
the past may break in the future.

Measures how much you could lose. It answers 'how bad can a bad day or bad month be?'

95% VaR of 2% means: on 95 out of 100 days the loss

The fan shows likely ranges. The middle line is the
median path, the edges are extreme cases.
Watch out
The simulation only reflects the assumptions you give it.
It is not a forecast of what will happen.

Testing, Limitations and Roadmap
Testing
The project has 23 automated test files (run with pytest). They check the core maths and exports:
Area
Test files
Returns, metrics,
drawdown
test_returns, test_metrics, test_drawdown
Risk and volatility
test_risk_metrics, test_rolling, test_garch, test_estimators
Statistics
test_summary, test_distributions, test_correlation, test_pca, test_clustering,
test_stationarity, test_diagnostics, test_timeseries
Factors and pairs
test_factors, test_scores, test_pairs, test_cointegration, test_spread
Exports
test_csv, test_excel, test_pdf, test_reporting_pipeline
Honest limitations
• The pages themselves (the screens) are not covered by automatic tests.
• Strategies, optimisation, regime and simulation code have fewer direct tests.
• Data comes from free providers that may be slow or change without notice.
• Large page files make the code harder to maintain.
• Machine learning and deep learning results can change between runs and rarely beat simple baselines
by much.
• Regimes are labelled with the whole sample, so they describe history.
Roadmap ideas
• Add tests for every page and engine.
• Split the biggest pages into smaller parts.
• Add more data sources and a lock file for libraries.
• Add more markets, factor models and explanation tools for ML.
• Add user accounts to save settings and reports.
